imageCaption: Aaliyah's hands, flour-dusted, holding up a piece of dough while her family gathers around the kitchen table in the yellow house. In the background, the coral table is covered with ingredients. Through the open window, the neighborhood street is visible, decorated with colorful bunting left over from the dominoes tournament.
text:
Aaliyah stood in the yellow house's kitchen at 9:33 AM on a Saturday that was already 47 degrees and climbing, staring at the problem in front of her with the intensity usually reserved for temporal physics and family dysfunction.

The problem was: what did a family that had spent seventy-four days accidentally healing the world bring to a neighborhood potluck?

"It has to be something you invented," Marco had said. Something that tells us who you are.

The problem was: Aaliyah had never invented anything edible in her life. She could map glitches. She could name them. She could observe with the precision of a person trained by a journalist mother to notice what mattered. But cooking was Anthony's department. Luisana's department was coffee and asking questions that made people want to tell her the truth. Elijah's department was befriending things and somehow producing snacks from his pockets like he was a vending machine with questionable inventory control.

Aaliyah's department was supposed to be understanding how systems worked.

But maybe that was the answer.

"What if we made something that nobody expects?" she said aloud, which was how she usually started conversations with herself, which was how all her best ideas arrived in the world.

Sully lifted his head from his spot under the table, interested in the tone of her voice more than the content of her words.

"What if we made something that tastes like a glitch?" she continued. "Something that doesn't make sense individually but makes perfect sense together?"

"You're describing your father's cooking philosophy," Luisana said from the doorway, where she'd been standing long enough to be covered in humidity and determination. She had her journal tucked under her arm and her hair was in the specific configuration that meant she'd given up on weather and accepted she was going to be damp regardless. "That's literally just Anthony's arroz con pollo."

"No," Aaliyah said. "That's just more. I mean something where the flavors are contradictory but the contradiction is the point. Something that shouldn't work but does because the person making it believed it would work."

She could see it now—the way all her observations over the past seventy-four days could actually be useful. The way Marco in the colmadón had stacked flavors like they were telling a story. The way the Lisbon Luncheon Loop had tasted like repetition and longing. The way food in every city they'd visited had carried the weight of people deciding what mattered to them.

"Get everyone," she said to her mother. "I need to explain this first before I start cooking, or it's just going to be chaos, and this chaos needs to be intentional."

Fifteen minutes later, the kitchen was packed with Gomezes and Gomez-adjacent family, which was to say: Anthony was at the table with his license plate collection spread in front of him like he was looking for something specific; Luisana was standing close enough to help but far enough away to observe; Elijah was dangling a piece of dried mango toward Sully, which was against all kitchen rules but nobody had the energy to argue about it at 9:51 AM.

"Okay," Aaliyah said, pulling up a chair. "Here's the thing. We've been documenting glitches for seventy-four days. And I know why they happen, or at least some of why—emotional resonance, genuine human chaos, the specific frequency that our family generates when we're together and real with each other. But I've been thinking about what that actually tastes like."

She pulled out a piece of paper where she'd written notes about the glitches they'd experienced. "The Lisbon Luncheon Loop tasted like tradition repeating. The Oslo Overlap tasted like two moments trying to occupy the same space. The Tokyo Temporal Tremor tasted like precision fighting against spontaneity."

"You haven't actually tasted any glitches," Elijah pointed out reasonably.

"Not literally," Aaliyah said. "But I've watched them. And I've watched what happens when we stabilize them. We don't do anything special. We just exist. We cook. We talk. We're weird together. And the glitches calm down because something about that frequency makes sense to the timeline."

She spread her hands. "What if we made a dish that tastes like that? What if we took flavors that don't usually go together—the way our family doesn't usually go together—and made them work because we believed they would?"

Anthony looked up from his license plates. He had that expression on his face that meant an idea had just relocated his entire internal organization. "You want to make something that tastes like us."

"I want to make something that tastes like what happens when temporal physics meets a family that books flights without asking," Aaliyah said. "I want to make something that tells the neighborhood: this is what stability tastes like when you stop trying to plan it and start building it."

Luisana smiled. It was the smile of a woman who'd spent the previous evening writing journal entries about growth and belonging and had just watched her daughter internalize those entries and convert them into something edible.

"What did you have in mind?" she asked.

"Mofongo," Aaliyah said. "But not the traditional kind. I want to make the base of it—the plantain, the garlic, the broth—but I want to add something that doesn't belong there. Something sweet. Something sour. Something that changes what the foundation is."

"Like what?" Elijah asked, which was his way of asking if this was going to work.

"Like," Aaliyah said slowly, "tamarind. And coconut. And lime. And maybe honey. I'm going to make a mofongo that tastes like traveling—like every place we've been, compressed into something you can eat. And it's going to taste like chaos and precision at the same time. And someone is going to try it at the potluck and they're going to understand that this family doesn't belong to places the way most families do. We belong to moments. And now we're choosing to build one."

The kitchen went very quiet.

Then Anthony stood up and hugged her, which wasn't surprising because Anthony hugged frequently, but it had the weight of him understanding exactly what his daughter had just done. She'd taken their entire life philosophy and compressed it into a recipe.

"We're going to need plantains," Luisana said, already pulling out her wallet. "I'll go to Marco's. He'll know where to get the good ones."

"I'll help," Elijah announced, which was his way of inviting himself on any errand that involved talking to people and possibly acquiring snacks.

"I'll stay," Anthony said. "Aaliyah, you're going to teach me this recipe. And I'm going to watch you not follow it exactly because you never do. And then we're going to figure out what you did that made it actually work. That's how you know something is important—when it only works because you did it your specific way."

And Aaliyah understood, standing in the kitchen with her father and the humidity and the weight of a neighborhood waiting to see if a family would show up on Saturday with something that meant something, that this was what it meant to belong somewhere.

Not to get it right.

But to get it right in a way that was uniquely, completely, unmistakably yours.

Sully barked once—not an alarm bark, just a satisfied bark, the bark of a dog who understood that important things were happening and his family was making them delicious.
